summary: Working in Buddhist and religious studies, Nyanabodhi studied under traditional teacher Ayya Khema and later succeeded her.

A Buddhist studies scholar, Nyanaponika Thera studied at the University of Peradeniya, under Nyanatiloka Mahathera in 1937, and under Mahasi Sayadaw around 1952–1953. He founded the Buddhist Publication Society, serving as director/editor (1958–1984) and president (~1958–1988).

Specializing in Tibetology, Nyingcha Duoji studied at Boston University and completed a PhD at Harvard University (attested 2014) under doctoral supervisor Leonard van der Kuijp and teacher Mark Elliott.

Nyo Shul Lungtok Tenpé Gyaltsen studied under Patrul Rinpoche (~1855–1887), Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso, and Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo. He also taught Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso and Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö.

A scholar in Buddhist studies and Tibetology, he studied at Katok and Nyoshul monasteries and under teachers including Dudjom Rinpoche, Dilgo Khyentse, Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö, Penor Rinpoche, and Khenpo Ngawang Pelzang.
Nyoten Jinbo was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Baisen Azegami and served as a professor at Komazawa University.

Active in Buddhist studies and Tibetology, Ogyen Trinley Dorje studied under Khenchen Thrangu Rinpoche (2000), Tenzin Gyatso (~2000), Bokar Rinpoche (~2000–2004), Drub Pön Dechen Rinpoche, Dragpa Tenpa Yarpel, and Pema Donyo Nyinje.

Specializing in Iranian and Central Asian studies and linguistics, Olaf Hansen held posts at the University of Berlin (~1937–1944), the University of Jena (~1944–1945), and the Free University of Berlin (~1950–1969).

A scholar of linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology, Hackstein studied at the University of Freiburg, University of Pennsylvania, and MLU Halle-Wittenberg. He held posts at Pennsylvania, Halle-Wittenberg, the University of Munich, and EPHE.

A specialist in Buddhist studies, Indology, and linguistics, Ole Holten Pind earned his doctorate at the University of Vienna (~2004–2009) under Ernst Steinkellner and served as a professor at the University of Hamburg.

Specializing in history and archaeology, Grabar studied at the University of Paris, Harvard, and Princeton. He served at the Albright Institute (~1953–1954), University of Michigan (1954–1969), Harvard (1969–1990), and the Institute for Advanced Study (1990–1998).

Working in history, archaeology, and Indology, Oliver Codrington served as Secretary of the Asiatic Society of Mumbai (attested 1878) and Honorary Librarian of the Royal Asiatic Society (attested 1892).

An Indology and Buddhist studies scholar, he studied at the University of Ceylon and SOAS under William Stede and Betty Heimann. He held faculty positions at the University of Ceylon, Pennsylvania, Harvard, and Smith College.
Active in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, Oliver Petersen studied under Geshe Thubten Ngawang (~1983–2003) and held a post at Tibetisches Zentrum Hamburg (~1993).
Working in Indology and philosophy, Oliver Philipp Frey studied at the University of Vienna and held a post there.

A scholar of Indology, philosophy, and religious studies, Lacombe studied at the École Normale Supérieure and the Faculty of Arts of Paris, where he later taught (~1947–1970) before holding a post at Paris-Sorbonne University (~1970–1974).
Working in Buddhist and religious studies, Olivier de Bernon studied under Pierre L. Lamant and held a post at the École Française d'Extrême-Orient (~1991).

Working in Indology, religious studies, and philosophy, Qvarnström studied at the University of Washington, Harvard, and Copenhagen, and under Tord Olsson. He held a post as responsible publisher at Lund University (attested 2000–2007).

Working in history, archaeology, and Indology, Prakash earned his PhD from the University of Delhi under Dasharatha Sharma. He held posts at Kirori Mal College (attested 1961) and as professor of economic history at Delhi (attested 2003).
A Sinology scholar, On Shionoya studied at Tokyo Imperial University (~1899–1902) and the University of Leipzig (~1906–1909), later holding a post at Tokyo Imperial University (~1920–1939).
